Proponents and opponents of the proposed rules and regulations both urge us to recognize these developments, although their respective assessments of the ramifications of these changes on the geographic scope of the section 203(b)(8) exemption differ. Certain parties speak in terms of Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas (SMSA) and Bureau of Census Urbanized Areas. Other parties describe contemporary urban areas as a hub or central business district rimmed by economically interrelated suburban communities, with modern transportation networks serving as the connecting "spokes." Still others, such as the Short Haul Committee, contend that the "multi-nucleated concept" best depicts the current urban model. It is incumbent upon us to be attuned to these developments in our delineation of the present day geographic limits of commercial zones.
Any interpretation of the scope of the commercial zone exemption must necessarily adhere to the meaning of the statutory terms of section 203(b)(8). It is in this regard that certain parties argue that the proposed augmentation of commercial zones is antithetical to the legislative intent of that statutory section. More specifically, it is asserted that introductory remarks to the Motor Carrier Act of 1935, made by Senator Wheeler, then Chairman of the Committee on Interstate Commerce, indicate that the exemption should only apply to "intramunicipal or occasional operations."
